title: The seven calls that make a connection
objective: By the end of this lesson you can name every call a client and a server make, explain what each one actually does, and write the address setup correctly on the first attempt.

blocks.text: The socket interface has been essentially unchanged for decades, and it is small: a client makes three calls, a server makes four. Learning what each one changes about the socket's state is enough to write correct network code and to read anyone else's.

blocks.text: Note where the asymmetry is: a client does not bind, because it does not care which local port it gets — the kernel picks a free one. A server binds because clients must know where to find it.

blocks.title: Two mistakes that cost hours
blocks.text: Forgetting htons on the port is the first: the connection goes to a port nobody is listening on, and the error gives no hint. Forgetting to zero the address structure is the second: leftover stack contents in an unset field produce behaviour that varies between runs. Both are silent, and both are avoided by writing the structure the way shown above every time.

listen() does not wait for anything. It marks the socket as passive and creates a queue for connections the kernel has completed but the program has not yet accepted. The second argument is how deep that queue may be.

blocks.title: The backlog is a queue depth, not a connection limit
blocks.text: It bounds how many completed connections may wait for accept(), not how many the server can serve. If the program accepts promptly, a small backlog is fine; if it is slow, a large one only delays the point at which clients are refused. Verified on one system: SOMAXCONN, the ceiling the kernel applies, was 4096. Passing a larger number silently gets clamped to it.

blocks.caption: Where the connection actually comes into being
lines: /* Server: returns a NEW descriptor for this one connection.
The listening socket stays open and keeps accepting. */
/* Client: this is the call that performs the handshake. */
perror("connect");   /* refused, timed out, unreachable — see the error lesson */

blocks.text: The most common misunderstanding here is thinking accept() returns the listening socket. It returns a new descriptor for one connection; the listener is untouched and continues to accept. Confusing the two is what leads to a server that serves exactly one client and then stops.

blocks.title: Write both halves
steps: Write a server: socket, SO_REUSEADDR, bind to loopback, listen, accept, print the peer address, close
Write a client: socket, connect, then close
Run the server, then the client, and confirm the peer address printed matches what ss shows
Deliberately omit htons on the port in the client and observe the failure
Deliberately skip zeroing the address structure and run it several times
Remove SO_REUSEADDR, connect once, kill the server, and restart it immediately — observe the bind failure
Put SO_REUSEADDR back and confirm the restart now succeeds
Run: ss -tlnp | grep <your port>    while the server is listening
blocks.expected: A working pair, and three failures you produced on purpose: a connection to the wrong port, behaviour that varies between runs, and a bind that fails on restart. Those three account for a large share of the time people lose writing their first socket program.

cheatsheet: Server: socket, bind, listen, accept. Client: socket, connect. Both: read/write, close
A client does not bind — the kernel assigns a free local port
AF_INET 2, AF_INET6 10, SOCK_STREAM 1, SOCK_DGRAM 2 — always use the names
Zero the address structure, set the family, and htons the port
INADDR_ANY listens on every interface; INADDR_LOOPBACK on this machine only
inet_pton converts text to an address and returns 1 on success — check it
listen() sets a queue depth, not a connection limit; SOMAXCONN was 4096 on one system
accept() returns a NEW descriptor; the listener keeps listening
Set SO_REUSEADDR before bind, or restarting the server fails

choices.B: A new descriptor for one connection, leaving the listener free to accept more

checkpoint.explanation: Treating the return value as the listener is what produces a server that handles exactly one client and then stops accepting.

checkpoint.prompt: A client connects to port 8080 but reaches nothing, and the server is definitely listening. What is the first thing to check?

choices.B: Whether htons was applied to the port — without it the bytes are in the wrong order and the port number is different

checkpoint.explanation: It is the most common first-time bug and it fails silently: the connection goes to a real but different port, so the error says only that nothing is listening there.

checkpoint.prompt: What does the second argument to listen() control?

choices.A: The maximum number of clients the server may serve
choices.B: How many completed connections may queue waiting for accept()

checkpoint.explanation: It bounds the waiting queue, not the total served. The kernel also caps it — measured as 4096 on one system — so a larger value is silently clamped.

checkpoint.prompt: Restarting your server immediately after stopping it fails with 'address already in use'. What is the fix?

choices.C: Use a different port each time

checkpoint.explanation: The address is held while previously open connections finish closing. That one setsockopt call, placed before bind, removes the problem entirely.
